khatm-i-khwajagan-naqshbandi-group-dhikr.name: Khatm-i Khwajagan (Naqshbandi group dhikr)
khatm-i-khwajagan-naqshbandi-group-dhikr.summary: A set Naqshbandi litany of Qur'an recitation, blessings on the Prophet and silent or vocal remembrance, recited together under a shaykh's guidance.

steps.text: A set Naqshbandi litany of Qur'an recitation, blessings on the Prophet and silent or vocal remembrance, recited together under a shaykh's guidance.

weekly-parashah-reflection-neo-hasidic.name: Weekly parashah reflection (neo-Hasidic)
weekly-parashah-reflection-neo-hasidic.summary: Each week read the Torah portion with a Hasidic commentary in mind and look for the inward, devotional teaching it holds for this week of your life.

steps.text: Each week read the Torah portion with a Hasidic commentary in mind and look for the inward, devotional teaching it holds for this week of your life.

calming-and-contemplation-zhiguan.name: Calming and contemplation (zhiguan)
calming-and-contemplation-zhiguan.summary: First calm the mind (zhi) by settling the breath and posture. Then contemplate (guan) any present thought as simultaneously empty, provisionally existing, and the middle, which are the threefold truth. Zhiyi's Mohe zhiguan sets out four kinds of samadhi practice (constant sitting, constant walking, half-walking half-sitting, and neither).

rudi-s-double-breath.name: Rudi's double breath
rudi-s-double-breath.summary: Breathe in, bringing attention down from the throat into the heart, and then down to the navel and the base of the body. Breathing out, let the energy rise up the spine. Keep the movement gentle and continuous, and return to the heart when attention scatters.

steps.text: Breathe in, bringing attention down from the throat into the heart, and then down to the navel and the base of the body. Breathing out, let the energy rise up the spine. Keep the movement gentle and continuous, and return to the heart when attention scatters.

khecari-mudra-historical-description-onl.name: Khecarī mudrā (historical description only)
khecari-mudra-historical-description-onl.summary: Described in haṭha texts as turning the tongue back and up into the cavity above the soft palate, sometimes after gradually lengthening the tongue. We list it for context: the full form involves cutting the frenum and is not something to try from a video.

steps.text: Described in haṭha texts as turning the tongue back and up into the cavity above the soft palate, sometimes after gradually lengthening the tongue. We list it for context: the full form involves cutting the frenum and is not something to try from a video.

sources.cite: Mallinson, The Khecarīvidyā (DPhil); no short clip on file.

dream-yoga-first-steps.name: Dream yoga, first steps
dream-yoga-first-steps.summary: During the day, keep reminding yourself "this is a dream" so that the habit carries into sleep. Before sleep, set a strong intention to recognise dreams. Visualise a luminous syllable at the throat as you fall asleep. Each morning, review whether you recognised a dream, and renew the intention.

feeding-your-demons-a-modern-adaptation-.name: Feeding your demons (a modern adaptation of Chöd)
feeding-your-demons-a-modern-adaptation-.summary: Find a struggle, such as fear or a craving, and feel where it lives in the body. Picture it as a figure in front of you and ask what it wants and what it really needs. Then imagine dissolving your body into nectar that gives it exactly that, until it is satisfied. Rest in the open space that remains.

the-view-from-above-spiritual-exercise.name: The view from above (spiritual exercise)
the-view-from-above-spiritual-exercise.summary: In imagination, rise above your situation until your concerns appear in the scale of the cosmos; return with a lighter, more just sense of what matters. One of the ancient "spiritual exercises" Pierre Hadot described.

steps.text: In imagination, rise above your situation until your concerns appear in the scale of the cosmos; return with a lighter, more just sense of what matters.

hermetic-ascent-and-rebirth-corpus-herme.name: Hermetic ascent and rebirth (Corpus Hermeticum XIII)
hermetic-ascent-and-rebirth-corpus-herme.summary: Read slowly and as contemplation, not just as information: the treatise guides the reader to put away the "torments" of matter and be reborn as the intellect praising God in silence.

steps.text: Read slowly and as contemplation, not just as information: the treatise guides the reader to put away the "torments" of matter and be reborn as the intellect praising God in silence.

active-imagination-imaginal-attention.name: Active imagination / imaginal attention
active-imagination-imaginal-attention.summary: Stay with an image (from a dream, a text or a place) as a living presence; let it speak and move; respond to it honestly rather than interpreting it away. In Corbin's terms it is a perception of the mundus imaginalis.

neelakantha-meditation.name: Neelakantha Meditation (mantra-based)
neelakantha-meditation.summary: This is an initiated mantra practice: the mantra is received from an authorised teacher. In outline, one sits twice a day, repeats the given mantra inwardly and lets it become subtle, treating the body as a stable platform rather than an obstacle. Learn it from the school; we describe it only so users know what the clips refer to.

nyasa.name: Nyāsa — placing mantra on the body
nyasa.summary: Touch or attend to specific points of the body (heart, head, crown, arms) while silently repeating the syllables assigned to them, so the body is treated as a seat of the deity before worship or meditation. Traditionally learnt with the specific mantra from a teacher.

steps.text: Touch or attend to specific points of the body (heart, head, crown, arms) while silently repeating the syllables assigned to them, so the body is treated as a seat of the deity before worship or meditation.
Traditionally learnt with the specific mantra from a teacher.

twelve-kalis.name: Contemplating the Twelve Kālīs (Krama)
twelve-kalis.summary: Take one Kālī of the Krama sequence at a time (e.g. Sṛṣṭikālī, the Kālī of creation). Study what phase of cognition she stands for — an object arising, being held, being withdrawn into the knower — and watch that phase in your own experience during the day.

metta-loving-kindness.name: Mettā (loving-kindness)
metta-loving-kindness.summary: Wish well to yourself, then a benefactor, a friend, a neutral person, a difficult person and finally all beings, using simple phrases or a felt sense of goodwill, letting it spread in every direction.

body-sweeping-goenka-vipassana.name: Body sweeping (Goenka vipassanā)
body-sweeping-goenka-vipassana.summary: After a few days of ānāpāna to sharpen attention, move attention systematically through the body from head to feet, observing every sensation with equanimity, as taught in ten-day residential courses.

yoga-nidra.name: Yoga nidrā
yoga-nidra.summary: Lying down, rotate awareness through the body, then breath, opposite sensations and visualisations while staying awake, ending with a personal resolve (saṅkalpa).

five-points-of-yoga-sivananda.name: Five points of yoga (Sivananda)
five-points-of-yoga-sivananda.summary: Proper exercise (āsana), proper breathing (prāṇāyāma), proper relaxation, proper diet and positive thinking with meditation, as summarised by Swami Vishnudevananda.

breath-centred-individually-adapted-asan.name: Breath-centred, individually adapted āsana (viniyoga)
breath-centred-individually-adapted-asan.summary: Link every movement to a slow inhale or exhale and adapt sequence, length and intensity to the person's body, age and aims, as taught by Krishnamacharya and T. K. V. Desikachar.

shamatha-with-object.name: Calm abiding with a support
shamatha-with-object.summary: Sit upright and relaxed. Rest your attention lightly on a simple support, such as the breath at the nostrils, a pebble, or a sound. When you notice the mind has wandered, return to the support without scolding yourself. Aim for many short, clear sessions rather than a few long, dull ones. Over time, loosen your grip until attention rests on its own.

tonglen.name: Tonglen (sending and taking)
tonglen.summary: Flash briefly on open, spacious mind. Then breathe in a feeling of heaviness and heat, and breathe out a feeling of coolness and light. Start with a real person who is suffering, perhaps yourself, and breathe in their pain while breathing out relief. Widen this to everyone who feels the same. Keep it simple and close to how you actually feel.

lojong-slogans.name: Mind training (lojong) slogans
lojong-slogans.summary: Choose one of the 59 slogans of Atisha's Seven Points, such as "Drive all blames into one". Carry it through the day. When irritation or self-cherishing comes up, recall the slogan and look again at the situation. Review the day each evening.

nine-breathings.name: Nine breathings of purification
nine-breathings.summary: Visualise the three channels: a central blue channel with a white one on the right and a red one on the left. Breathe in through the right nostril and out through the left three times, releasing anger. Then breathe in through the left and out through the right three times, releasing attachment. Finally, breathe in through both and push the breath up the central channel three times, releasing ignor

Finally, breathe in through both and push the breath up the central channel three times, releasing ignorance.
Rest afterwards.

zazen.name: Zazen posture and breath
zazen.summary: Sit on a cushion with your knees on the floor, or on a chair, with the spine upright. Rest the hands in the cosmic mudra, left on right with the thumbs lightly touching, and keep the eyes half-open and lowered. Breathe naturally through the nose. Beginners can count breaths from one to ten and start again whenever they lose count.

huatou.name: Huatou (critical phrase)
huatou.summary: Take up a short question, such as "What is wu?" or "Before my parents were born, what was my original face?" Keep asking it with a sense of genuine not-knowing until a "great doubt" gathers. Return to the question whenever you lose it. This is Sheng Yen's method, best done in retreat with guidance.

mindful-breathing-pv.name: Mindful breathing with gathas
mindful-breathing-pv.summary: Breathe in and silently say "In"; breathe out and say "Out". As you settle, shorten it to "Deep / Slow", "Calm / Ease" or "Smile / Release". Use a bell or a phone chime as a reminder to stop, breathe three times and come back to the body.

walking-meditation.name: Walking meditation
walking-meditation.summary: Walk slowly and coordinate your steps with your breath, for example two steps on the in-breath and three on the out-breath. Feel each foot touching the earth as if kissing it. You are not trying to arrive anywhere; every step is the arrival.

ajikan.name: Ajikan (A-syllable meditation)
ajikan.summary: Shingon practitioners visualise the Sanskrit syllable A on a moon disc above a lotus. The A signifies the unborn source of all things. They join it with the breath and expand the moon until it fills the universe, then contract it into the heart. Formal ajikan is taught after initiation; this entry is an orientation only.

video-lectio.name: Video lectio (short contemplative reading)
video-lectio.summary: Watch a short image or text slowly, then sit with a single phrase that stays with you before meditating.

welcoming-practice.name: Welcoming Practice
welcoming-practice.summary: When a strong reaction arises, feel it as a sensation in the body; say "welcome" to it instead of resisting; then let go of the desire for security, approval or control, and so release it into presence.

neoplatonic-contemplation.name: Neoplatonic contemplation ("strip away everything")
neoplatonic-contemplation.summary: Following Plotinus, turn attention from objects to the activity of knowing, then let even that subtle self-image fall away, resting in the simple presence it comes from. Usually practised after a period of calming meditation.

unio-mystica-letters.summary: Abulafia's path: combine and permute the Hebrew letters of divine names, with breath and pronunciation, to loosen ordinary thinking. Historically taught only under a teacher. Listed here for context, not as instruction.

middle-pillar-outline.name: The Middle Pillar (outline)
middle-pillar-outline.traditionLabel: Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn
middle-pillar-outline.summary: Stand or sit straight. Picture a slender pillar of light along the midline of the body. Bring attention to five centers in turn, seeing each as a sphere of its colour: brilliant white above the crown; soft lavender at the throat; rose pink at the heart; deep violet at the loins; and at the feet the four earth tones quartered. ease-through-the-body-trika-prep.name: Ease through the body with the breath (Trika prep)
ease-through-the-body-trika-prep.summary: Sit upright and let the breath settle into a comfortable rhythm. Notice where the breath is clearest and rest attention there. Let that sense of ease spread through the whole body, using the breath as a home base for steady attention. When the mind wanders, return gently to the breath without force. Close by sitting quietly for a few breaths and noticing the whole body at once.

vbt-sound-dissolution.name: Listening to the inner sound (VBT verses 38-39)
vbt-sound-dissolution.summary: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle by itself. Listen for a faint inner sound, a soft ringing or hum beneath the sounds of the room. Rest attention on it lightly, without straining to hear. Let it be loud, soft, present or absent; do not follow it into images or stories. When the mind wanders, come back to listening. vbt-body-as-consciousness.name: The body as awareness (VBT verse 63)
vbt-body-as-consciousness.summary: Sit and let attention rest on the whole body at once: not one part, the whole field of sensation. Then take the body, and the world around it, as made of awareness. Let this be felt rather than thought. When the mind narrows back to "me" and "mine", return to the wider field and rest there. The body stays where it is; only the sense of it being separate softens.

vbt-mind-between-objects.summary: First settle with the breath for a few minutes. Then notice the moment the mind lets go of one thing, a sensation, a thought, a sound, and before it takes up the next. Rest in that in-between. Do not chase the next object and do not push it away. When you find you have already moved on, come back to the gap. Practise the breath-pause sit first; this one needs a little steadiness.

vbt-space-contemplation.name: Spaciousness: a wall of skin with nothing inside (VBT verses 43-48)
vbt-space-contemplation.summary: Sit and notice the space of the room around you, the space that holds the walls and your body. Then sense the space inside the body: the chest, the mouth, the skull. Feel the skin as a thin wall with open space within and without. Let the inner and outer space be one field and rest in that openness. vbt-twelve-centres.name: Touching the end-of-twelve through the day (VBT verse 51)
vbt-twelve-centres.summary: This is a daily-life practice, not a sit. Several times a day, while walking, waiting or eating, let attention rest for a few breaths at the space just above the crown of the head, the "end of twelve", then carry on with what you were doing. Keep the touch light and brief. The remembering is the practice.

rebirth.label: Rebirth

takes.theravada: Craving and kamma drive a new birth, yet no unchanging self passes from life to life.
takes.tibetan: Between death and the next birth lies the bardo, where the mind meets its own nature and its habits.
takes.vedanta: The subtle body moves from life to life, carried by karma; the Self you are was never born and never dies.
takes.platonic: The soul is immortal and returns to new lives, choosing its next life by what it has become (the Myth of Er).
takes.anthroposophy: The human I returns through repeated earth lives, meeting the karma it has made and growing through it.
takes.krishnamurti: Asks what it is that would be reborn: the stream of memory called the self can end now, which matters more than a next life.

rebirth.intro: Does anything carry on after death, and if so, what? The Buddha said a stream of becoming continues without a fixed self. The Upanishads said the Self is untouched while the subtle body moves on. Plato told the Myth of Er. Theosophy and Steiner rebuilt the idea for the modern West. Start anywhere and keep going.

questions.label: What is reborn?
questions.blurb: If there is no fixed self, what links one life to the next? Consciousness, karma, a subtle body, a soul.

questions.label: Remembering past lives
questions.blurb: The Buddha's first knowledge on the night of awakening, children's memories, and why most of us forget.

questions.label: Karma and the next life
questions.blurb: How intention shapes what comes next, and what it would mean to take that seriously now.

questions.label: Between lives: the bardo
questions.blurb: The Tibetan map of the passage from death to birth, and practices for meeting it awake.

questions.label: The West: Er, Pythagoras, Steiner
questions.blurb: Plato's Myth of Er, the Pythagoreans, Plotinus, Kabbalah's gilgul, Theosophy and Anthroposophy.

questions.label: Dying and near-death
questions.blurb: What the dying, the near-dead and the people who sit with them report.

questions.label: Ending the round
questions.blurb: Liberation as the end of rebirth: nibbana, moksha, the deathless, no coming and no going.

kamma.label: Karma

takes.theravada: Kamma is intention: what you will and do shapes what you meet and who you become.
takes.tibetan: Actions ripen across lives; purification and merit change how they ripen, and wisdom uproots them.
takes.vedanta: Action binds as long as it is done for its fruits; action offered without attachment frees.
takes.kashmir-shaivism: Karma is one of the three impurities that veil consciousness; recognising your nature as Śiva dissolves it.
takes.kriya-yoga: Right action and meditation work out past karma; Kriya practice is taught as a way to hasten it.
takes.anthroposophy: Karma is a just weaving of destiny across lives, worked out in the meetings and trials of each new life.
takes.fourth-way: Most of what we call action is mechanical; only conscious effort is truly ours.

kamma.intro: Karma is intention, said the Buddha. The Gita says act, and let go of the fruit. The West rebuilt it as moral law and destiny.

questions.label: Karma as intention
questions.blurb: What makes an action skilful.

questions.label: Karma yoga
questions.blurb: Acting without clinging to the result.

questions.label: Results and destiny
questions.blurb: Fate, free will and the ripening of deeds.

self.label: Self & not-self

takes.theravada: Nothing you can point to as yours is a lasting self; seeing this ends the conceit 'I am'.
takes.zen: Study the self to forget the self: the self, like all things, has no fixed essence apart from everything else.
takes.tibetan: The self is empty of inherent existence; it exists only as a label placed on body and mind.
takes.vedanta: Ask 'Who am I?': under every thought is the one Self, pure awareness, which is Brahman.
takes.kashmir-shaivism: The self is Śiva, free consciousness; awakening is recognising what you already are.
takes.christian-mysticism: Let go of the self that clings, and God is found in the ground of the soul.
takes.fourth-way: We have no single permanent I, only many passing 'I's; a real I has to be built through work on oneself.
takes.krishnamurti: The self is a bundle of memory and reaction; to see it clearly, without a watcher, is freedom.

self/emptiness.label: Emptiness

For the Madhyamaka, nothing exists from its own side; for Zen, emptiness is this very moment; for Thich Nhat Hanh, it is interbeing; for Dzogchen, it is the open ground of mind. meditation.label: Meditation

takes.theravada: Restraint and right view first; then the mind settles and sees the arising and passing of things.
takes.zen: Just sit: practice is not a means to awakening but its expression.
takes.tibetan: Calm the mind, then recognise its nature: awareness itself, open and clear.
takes.vedanta: Quiet the mind through discipline or devotion, then rest as the awareness in which all experience comes and goes.
takes.kashmir-shaivism: Practices such as those of the Vijñāna Bhairava turn any moment of experience back to the consciousness it arises in.
takes.kriya-yoga: Breath and life-energy techniques still the mind and turn it inward, toward the divine.
takes.christian-mysticism: Contemplative prayer: rest in God beyond words and images.
takes.fourth-way: Self-remembering: be present to yourself in the middle of ordinary life.
takes.krishnamurti: Not a method but choiceless awareness: watching the movement of thought without a controller.

takes.theravada: Life as we grasp it is unsatisfying; see its cause and it can end.
takes.zen: Suffering is met, not escaped: held in mindful attention, it can be transformed.
takes.tibetan: Suffering comes from grasping at a self; seeing others suffer as we do is the root of compassion.
takes.vedanta: Suffering comes from taking yourself to be the body and mind.
takes.christian: Suffering can be carried and transformed, in communion with Christ's own.
takes.krishnamurti: Sorrow ends when you meet it completely, without escaping into explanation.

takes.theravada: Craving is the origin of suffering; when it fades, suffering ends.
takes.zen: Desire is met with open attention rather than fought; seen as empty, it loosens by itself.
takes.vedanta: Desire for the fruits of action keeps the wheel turning; the longing for liberation is the one desire worth keeping.
takes.platonic: Desire is redirected, not destroyed: love rises from beautiful things toward Beauty itself.
takes.christian-mysticism: Detachment: want nothing but God, and the soul is free.

death.label: Death

takes.theravada: Recollect death daily: it loosens clinging and shows the urgency of the path.
takes.zen: Birth and death are the life of the way itself; seen clearly, they lose their grip on the mind.
takes.tibetan: Death is a doorway: rightly prepared, the moment of dying can be the moment of liberation.
takes.vedanta: Death belongs to the body and the mind; find out who it is that fears it.
takes.platonic: Philosophy is practice for dying: the soul's training in turning from the body toward what is real.
takes.anthroposophy: After death the soul looks back on its life, is purified (kamaloca) and prepares for a new birth.
takes.krishnamurti: Die each day to what you know and hold; then death is not at the far end of life but within it.

awakening.label: Awakening

takes.theravada: Nibbāna is the ending of greed, hatred and delusion, reached through stages that cannot be lost.
takes.zen: Awakening is seeing your own nature, sudden or gradual, and then living it.
takes.tibetan: Buddhahood is the full recognition of the mind's own nature, wisdom and compassion inseparable.
takes.vedanta: Liberation is not gained; it is the end of the mistaken belief that you were ever bound.
takes.kashmir-shaivism: Liberation is recognition (pratyabhijñā): you have always been Śiva, free consciousness.
takes.neoplatonism: The soul turns inward and ascends until it is one with the One.
takes.christian-mysticism: Union with God, reached through love and letting go, in which the soul finds God in its own ground.
takes.fourth-way: We are asleep; waking up begins with seeing our own mechanicalness and remembering ourselves.

middle-pillar-week.title: Middle Pillar week
middle-pillar-week.intro: One outline, seven sittings. Each day adds one centre to the pillar, then rests in the circulation. Ten minutes a day. This is orientation only: the full form is learnt in the order or from a qualified teacher.
middle-pillar-week.author: wiser

units.title: The pillar
units.intro: The pillar first: light along the midline, crown to feet. Nothing else.

items.note: Can you feel the midline as one continuous line? If not, that is the work.

units.title: Crown
units.intro: Add the crown: brilliant white above the head, the source of the light.

items.note: White first: the colour of undifferentiated light.

units.title: Throat
units.intro: Add the throat: soft lavender, where the light narrows into speech.

items.note: Notice any pressure in the throat and breathe around it, never through force.

units.title: Heart
units.intro: Add the heart: rose pink, the largest sphere, the seat of the circulation.

items.note: The heart centre carries the practice. Give it the most time.

units.title: Loins
units.intro: Add the loins: deep violet, where the light gathers before descending.

items.note: Gathering is not grasping. Let the violet hold without pulling.

units.title: Feet
units.intro: Add the feet: the quartered earth tones grounding the whole pillar.

items.note: A pillar with no foundation is a fantasy. Feel the feet.

units.title: The circulation
units.intro: The whole week in one sit: five centres, then the circulation down the front and up the spine with the breath.

items.note: If the circuit runs on its own, let it. If not, return to the heart.

trika-prep-week.title: Trika prep week
trika-prep-week.intro: Seven days of foundation for Abhinavagupta and VBT study: steady breath, the turn of the breath, and recognition. Ten minutes a day. Initiated practices are not here: when the gap is steady, take the next step with a qualified teacher in the tradition.
trika-prep-week.author: wiser

units.title: Settle
units.intro: The home base: ease through the body with the breath.

items.note: Where is the breath clearest today? That is your seat for the week.

units.title: The turn
units.intro: Notice where the in-breath becomes the out-breath. Rest there; hold nothing.

items.note: Did you find the turning, or the idea of it? Either is fine — noted, not judged.

units.title: Recognition
units.intro: One sutra slowly, then look: does anything appear outside awareness?

items.note: Write one sentence on what recognition felt like versus what you thought about it.

units.title: Return to ease
units.intro: Same foundation, deeper seat. The gap work needs a rested body.

items.note: Compare today with day 1: steadier, sleepier, brighter? Log it plainly.

units.title: Longer turn
units.intro: Same gap practice, full sit. Let attention fall in; never force it.

items.note: If strain appears, drop back to ease. The gap is found, not made.

units.title: Recognition again
units.intro: Same contemplation, fresh experience. Sound, thought, feeling — inside or outside?

items.note: One line for the journal: what was recognised, and by what?

units.title: The week in one sit
units.intro: Ease, then the turn, then recognition — one short sit chaining all three in order.

items.note: Which of the three is your door? That is what you take to a teacher next.

vbt-foundations.title: VBT Foundations
vbt-foundations.intro: Seven contemplative practices from the Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra, in a progression from the breath to daily life (not the text's own order): the turn of the breath, the gap between objects, inner sound, the body as awareness, the sense spaces, spaciousness, and the end-of-twelve through the day. Each is a quiet sit you can do on your own. The rest of the text (breath retention, mantra, the subtle-body practices) is learned from a qualified teacher: when one of these becomes your door, take it to a teacher in the tradition.
vbt-foundations.author: wiser

units.title: Breath-pause
units.intro: The first practice the text presents: resting in the gap between the in-breath and the out-breath.

items.note: Did you find the turning, or the idea of it? Either is fine — noted, not judged.

units.title: The gap between thoughts
units.intro: When the mind lets go of one thing and before it takes up the next, rest in the middle. Build on day 1's steadiness.

items.note: How long was the gap today? One thought-width, or longer?

units.title: Inner sound
units.intro: Listen to the subtle inner sound until sound dissolves into silence.

items.note: What quality was the sound — ring, hum, tone, silence? Log it plainly.

units.title: Body as consciousness
units.intro: Conceive of the body — or the whole universe — as nothing but consciousness. A felt sense, not an idea.

items.note: Did the body-sense shift, or was it the same body with a different label? Both are data.

units.title: Inner and outer spaces
units.intro: A sense contact — the outer space where it arrives, the inner space where it is received, both as one field.

items.note: Which side did attention collapse into — inner or outer? That is the habit to notice.

units.title: Spaciousness
units.intro: The space of the room, the space inside the body, the skin as a thin wall between: one open field.

items.note: When did the mind grasp for something solid? What did it grasp at?

units.title: The end-of-twelve through the day
units.intro: Not a sitting practice. A few times today, let attention touch the space just above the crown for a breath or two, then carry on.

items.note: How many times today did you remember? The remembering is the practice, not the count.
